options.why: Assumed every number larger than $10$ must have more than two factors.
Confused $17$ with the special cases $0$ and $1$.

questions.solution_text:
The factors of $17$ are $1$ and $17$.
It has exactly two factors, so it is prime.

options.why: Checked that $27$ is odd but did not test the factor $3$.
Applied the special classification for $0$ and $1$ to $27$.

questions.solution_text:
$3 \times 9=27$
So $27$ has more than two factors and is composite.

options.why: Mistook one factor for the exactly two factors required for a prime.
Assumed every positive integer must be prime or composite.

questions.solution_text: $1$ has only one factor, so it is neither prime nor composite.

options.why: Ignored that a prime must be a positive integer with exactly two factors.
Treated being divisible by many nonzero numbers as the composite-number definition without requiring a positive integer.

questions.solution_text: $0$ is not a positive integer, so it is neither prime nor composite.

options.why: Assumed every number greater than $70$ has factors other than $1$ and itself.
Applied the special classification for $0$ and $1$ to $73$.

questions.solution_text:
$73$ is not divisible by $2$, $3$, $5$ or $7$. These are the only prime factors that need testing before the factor-pair partners pass each other.
The only positive factors are $1$ and $73$, so $73$ is prime.

options.why: Assumed that being odd makes $87$ prime and missed the factor pair $3 \times 29=87$.
Applied the special classification for $0$ and $1$ to $87$.

questions.solution_text:
$3 \times 29=87$
So $87$ has factors other than $1$ and itself and is composite.

options.why: Checked only whether $93$ is even and missed the factor pair $3 \times 31=93$.
Applied the special classification for $0$ and $1$ to $93$.

questions.solution_text:

So $93$ has factors other than $1$ and itself and is composite.

options.why: Stopped after checking divisibility by $2$, $3$, $5$ and $7$, missing the factor pair $11 \times 17=187$.
Applied the special classification for $0$ and $1$ to $187$.

questions.solution_text:
$11 \times 17=187$
So $187$ has factors other than $1$ and itself and is composite.

options.why: Applied the special classification for $0$ and $1$ to $12$.
Counted only $1$ and $12$ as factors and missed factors such as $2$ and $6$.

questions.solution_text:
$2 \times 6=12$
So $12$ has factors other than $1$ and itself and is composite.
